facts.statement: Scanisaurus lived during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period in what is now Sweden and Russia.
facts.quote: Scanisaurus is a dubious genus of plesiosaur that lived in what is now Sweden and Russia during the Campanian stage of the Late Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: The species Scanisaurus nazarowi was described in 1911 by Nikolay Bogolyubov based on a single vertebral centrum found near Orenburg, Russia.
facts.quote: The genus contains one species, S. nazarowi, described in 1911 by Nikolay Bogolyubov as a species of Cimoliasaurus based on a single vertebral centrum discovered near Orenburg, Russia.

facts.statement: Per-Ove Persson moved the species into its own genus in 1959 after observing differences between the Russian type centrum and new fossils from Skåne.
facts.quote: The genus contains one species, S. nazarowi, described in 1911 by Nikolay Bogolyubov as a species of Cimoliasaurus based on a single vertebral centrum discovered near Orenburg, Russia. the species was moved into its own genus by Per-Ove Persson in 1959 after several differences were observed between the Russian centra and new fossils from Skåne and the type species of Cimoliasaurus.

facts.statement: Scanisaurus was about 4 to 5 meters long and likely fed on small prey like fish or belemnites in both open water and on the sea floor.
facts.quote: Scanisaurus shared its environment with a diverse marine fauna, including many other marine reptiles. It would have been a middle trophic-level predator, about 4 – 5 m in length, and would have been able to feed both in open water and on the sea floor, likely feeding mainly on small prey such as small fish or belemnites.

facts.statement: A fountain featuring two sculptures of Scanisaurus was erected in the Swedish town of Bromölla in 1971.
facts.quote: A fountain bearing the name of the animal and featuring two sculptures depicting it was erected in the Swedish town of Bromölla in 1971.

facts.statement: Nikolay Bogolyubov described a Late Cretaceous posterior cervical vertebra discovered near Orenburg, Russia, in 1911.
facts.quote: In 1911, Russian paleontologist Nikolay Bogolyubov described a Late Cretaceous posterior cervical (neck) vertebral centrum discovered near Orenburg, Russia.

facts.statement: Bogolyubov distinguished the new species by noting its centrum was wider than those of other Cimoliasaurus specimens.
facts.quote: The main distinguishing feature used by Bogolyubov to justify the creation of a new species was that his centrum was wider than other centra referred to Cimoliasaurus.

facts.statement: Per-Ove Persson examined plesiosaur fossils from Late Cretaceous Skåne in 1959, primarily from the Kristianstad Basin and the island of Ivö.
facts.quote: In 1959, Swedish paleontologist Per-Ove Persson examined the fragmentary plesiosaur fossil record of Late Cretaceous Skåne in southern Sweden, primarily recovered from fossil sites within the Kristianstad Basin (many from the island of Ivö) and from south-western Skåne.

facts.statement: Per-Ove Persson named the new genus Scanisaurus, which means "Skåne lizard".
facts.quote: Persson named this new genus Scanisaurus, meaning "Skåne lizard".

facts.statement: Per-Ove Persson concluded that Scanisaurus was the most common plesiosaur in Late Cretaceous Skåne because its vertebrae were far more common than those of other species.
facts.quote: Because centra referred to S. cf. nazarowi were far more common in the Swedish fossil sites compared to centra from other plesiosaurs, Persson concluded that S. cf. nazarowi was "obviously the most common plesiosaurian" in Late Cretaceous Skåne.

facts.statement: In 1996, Per-Ove Persson provisionally assigned a crushed skull from the Ignaberga quarry to Scanisaurus based on matching tooth striation patterns.
facts.quote: In 1996, Persson provisionally referred a crushed reptile skull recovered from Ignaberga quarry in the Kristianstad Basin to Scanisaurus sp., since two tooth fragments associated with the fossil showed the same striation pattern as in the teeth referred to S. cf. nazrowi.

facts.statement: The only cranial fossil referred to Scanisaurus suggests it had a comparatively larger head than other long-necked plesiosaurs.
facts.quote: Though the skull is too crushed to give much useful anatomical information, it is the only cranial fossil referred to Scanisaurus (with the exception of teeth) and demonstrates that its head was comparatively larger than the heads of other dolichodiran plesiosaurs.

facts.statement: Scanisaurus was a long-necked plesiosaur with a neck shorter than that of some relatives like Elasmosaurus.
facts.quote: Scanisaurus was a "dolichodiran" (i.e. long-necked) plesiosaur, albeit one with a neck relatively shorter than those of some of its relatives (such as Elasmosaurus).

facts.statement: Per-Ove Persson suggested Scanisaurus might represent a new family of plesiosaurs intermediate between polycotylids and elasmosaurids.
facts.quote: Persson suggested that Scanisaurus could be a representative of a new family of Late Cretaceous plesiosaurs, possibly a group intermediate between pliosaurs such as the polycotylids and elasmosaurids.

facts.statement: In 1960, Per-Ove Persson placed both Cimoliasaurus and Scanisaurus in the family Cimoliasauridae.
facts.quote: In 1960, Persson referred both Cimoliasaurus and Scanisaurus to a new family of mesodiran plesiosaurs, which he dubbed the Cimoliasauridae.

facts.statement: A 2009 revision showed that Cimoliasaurus belongs to the Elasmosauridae, making the family Cimoliasauridae synonymous with Elasmosauridae.
facts.quote: A 2009 revision of the type fossils of Cimoliasaurus by American paleontologist F. Robin O'Keefe and Canadian paleontologist Hallie P. Street showed that Cimoliasaurus belonged to the Elasmosauridae, making the Cimoliasauridae synonymous with the Elasmosauridae.

facts.statement: A 2011 re-examination suggested that placing Scanisaurus in the Elasmosauridae was plausible.
facts.quote: A 2011 re-examination of the cervical vertebrae referred to Scanisaurus by Swiss paleontologist Christian Foth and German paleontologists Johannes Kalbe and René Kautz suggested that Scanisaurus being placed in the Elasmosauridae was plausible.

facts.statement: Modern research generally places Scanisaurus in the Elasmosauridae, though its exact position within the family remains uncertain.
facts.quote: Modern research thus tends to place Scanisaurus in the Elasmosauridae, though its precise position within the family is uncertain.

facts.statement: The genus Scanisaurus is considered of questionable validity due to limited type material and a lack of diagnostic features, though it is still used in practice.
facts.quote: Due to the limited type material and the lack of diagnostic features in the Swedish fossils confidently separating Scanisaurus from other Late Cretaceous elasmosaurids, the genus is of questionable validity, though it continues to be used in practice.

facts.statement: Per-Ove Persson noted that the species remained "undefinable" because it was based on only a single vertebral centrum, yet he felt confident the Swedish material belonged to it.
facts.quote: Persson noted that S. nazarowi remained an "undefinable" species since it remains based on only a single vertebral centrum, but felt confident that the Swedish material was referrable to the species since it did not differ in any essential points from Bogolyubov's fossil.

facts.statement: Most fossils of Scanisaurus cf. nazarowi have been recovered from the Kristianstad Basin, where they represent the most common plesiosaur fossils found.
facts.quote: Most of the fossils referred to Scanisaurus cf. nazarowi have been recovered from fossil sites within the Kristianstad Basin, where, according to Persson, S. cf. nazarowi fossils represent the most common plesiosaur fossils found.

facts.statement: The species S. nazarowi was described in 1911 by Nikolay Bogolyubov based on a single vertebral centrum discovered near Orenburg, Russia.
facts.quote: El género contiene una especie, S. nazarowi, descrita en 1911 por Nikolay Bogolyubov como una especie de Cimoliasaurus basada en un solo centro vertebral descubierto cerca de Orenburgo, Rusia.

facts.statement: Scanisaurus is a dubious genus name of a plesiosaur that lived in what is now Sweden and Russia during the Late Cretaceous Campanian.
